meta.blurb: Everyone around you wants you to fit in. In an essay from 1841, Ralph Waldo Emerson says the opposite. Trust yourself, stop copying other people and do your own work, because nothing else can bring you peace.
meta.bible: Ralph Waldo Emerson: American essayist and lecturer (1803 to 1882), a former Unitarian minister who lived in Concord, Massachusetts. Self-Reliance: an essay published in 1841 in Essays: First Series. Famous ideas, all attributed to Emerson: Trust thyself, every heart vibrates to that iron string; whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist; a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds; to be great is to be misunderstood; envy is ignorance and imitation is suicide; insist on yourself, never imitate; the roses under my window live in the present; the soul is no traveller; society is a wave; do your work and I shall know you; nothing can bring you peace but yourself. People Emerson names as misunderstood: Pythagoras, Socrates, Jesus, Luther, Copernicus, Galileo, Newton. An institution is the lengthened shadow of one man (examples: Luther's Reformation, Wesley's Methodism). Scipio: a Roman general. Naples, Rome: cities Emerson imagines travelling to. Voice and tone: a bracing, direct, encouraging essay retold in our own words, respectful of religion, and never telling anyone to be unkind.

B1B2: Ralph Waldo Emerson published his essay Self-Reliance in 1841, in a book called Essays: First Series. It is a short and powerful call to every reader to trust his own mind.
Emerson begins with an observation: we often push aside our own best thoughts simply because they are ours. Later, when we read them in a great book, we recognise them and wish we had trusted them.
He says that in every work of genius we meet our own rejected thoughts, which come back to us looking grander. Great writers and artists teach us to respect what we first felt.

For Emerson, to believe that what is true in your own heart is true for everyone is the mark of genius. So he urges us to speak our private convictions boldly, because they may turn out to be shared by all.
Trust yourself, he writes, because every heart vibrates to that iron string. He asks us to accept the place, the time and the people that life has given us.

All the great people of the past trusted their own thoughts, and they did the work that was truly theirs. Emerson says that we should stand in the same spirit, and not hide behind the opinions of others.
To show what he means, Emerson points to babies and small children. They are free from the need to please, and they live exactly as they feel.
A healthy boy says what he thinks, and he does not care who likes it. Grown-up people lose this freedom, because they begin to worry about how they look to others.
Emerson then says that society is always working against the independence of its members. It is like a company in which everyone agrees to give up his freedom in return for safety.
The virtue that the world asks for most is conformity, which means doing what everyone else does. Self-reliance is the thing that society dislikes, because it refuses to follow the crowd.
Anyone who wants to be a real person, Emerson says, must be a nonconformist. Nothing is more sacred than the honesty of your own mind.
Emerson remembers an older friend who warned him that his inner impulses might be wrong. He answered that they did not seem wrong to him, and he would follow what he found true.
He says that he cannot accept a rule simply because other people accept it. Each rule must pass the test of his own conscience before he will call it good.
Emerson is ashamed to see how easily people bow to labels, big groups and customs that have lost their life. He wants us to look at the thing itself, and not only at its name.
It is easy to trust yourself when you are alone, and easy to follow the crowd when you are in it. The great person, says Emerson, keeps the independence of solitude even in the middle of a crowd.
Emerson is also doubtful about kind acts that people do only because it is the fashion. He wants kindness to come from real feeling, and he says that goodness should be firm as well as soft.
Following customs that you no longer believe in only wastes your strength, says Emerson. It makes our actions look empty, because they no longer come from what we truly think.
A person who belongs to a party or a sect becomes easy to predict. As Emerson points out, if he knows your group, he can guess your argument before you speak.
Those who do not conform are often punished by the displeasure of the world. So a man must learn to weigh a sour face for what it is worth, and not to fear it.
Many people are afraid to change their minds because they want to look consistent. Emerson says that a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.
Speak what you think today in strong words, and tomorrow speak what you think then, even if it disagrees with today. A mind that is honest will change as it learns, and that is no shame.

Is it so bad to be misunderstood, he asks, when so many great people have been? Pythagoras, Socrates, Jesus, Luther, Copernicus, Galileo and Newton were all misunderstood, and to be great, Emerson says, is to be misunderstood.

Emerson says that a life is not a straight line, and that a good life may look confused up close. The voyage of the best ship is a zigzag of a hundred turns, yet from far away the line looks straight.
He says that we should live for ourselves and not as a show for other people. A plain and honest life is better than a bright life that cannot keep steady.
When your actions are truly your own, they explain themselves. Each honest action also helps to explain all the other honest actions that you have done.
Emerson says that every great person is different from all the others. The part that made him great is exactly the part that he could not borrow from anyone.

There comes a time, Emerson says, when everyone must decide that envy is ignorance and that imitation is a kind of suicide. We must accept ourselves, for better or worse, and work the piece of ground that was given to us.
So he tells us to insist on ourselves and never to imitate. We can give our own gift with the force of a whole life, but a borrowed talent is only half ours.
The roses under his window, Emerson says, make no reference to older roses or to better ones. They are what they are, and they live fully in today.
Unlike the roses, we look back at the past with regret or stand on tiptoe to see the future. Emerson says that we cannot be strong and happy until we, too, live in the present.

Emerson trusts the first quick sense of what is true, which he calls instinct or intuition. He says that we do not get this sense from other people, because it comes from a place deeper than argument.
Emerson also writes about prayer in a way that surprises many readers. He thinks the best prayer is not a request for small favours, but a calm look at life from the highest point.
In Emerson's view, constant discontent is a sign of weakness, which he calls a lack of self-reliance. A person who keeps complaining has not yet learned to trust his own will.
Emerson says that an institution is the lengthened shadow of one man. A great movement, such as Luther's Reformation or Wesley's Methodism, began as one person's strong idea.
Next, Emerson turns to travel, which he calls a fool's paradise when it is done to escape ourselves. He does not object to travel for study or art, but he says the soul is no traveller.

A man who travels to be amused, or to find what he does not carry within, is only travelling away from himself. Emerson imagines sailing to Naples and waking up to find the same sad self lying beside him.
Emerson says that our minds travel even when our bodies are forced to stay at home. We imitate other countries and other people, he adds, and imitation is only the travelling of the mind.
Emerson also warns against putting too much trust in property and money. He says that people judge each other by what each one has, and not by what each one is.
Emerson says that people often value schools, churches and laws mainly as guards of property. A person who relies on himself does not need to lean on them in the same way.
Next, he says something that surprises many people: society never really moves forward. It loses on one side as fast as it gains on the other, so a change is not always an improvement.
The modern man has built a coach, but he has lost the use of his feet. He has a fine watch, but he cannot tell the time by the sun.
Society is like a wave, Emerson says, which moves forward while the water that forms it stays where it is. The people of a country are not made better just because their time has new tools.
Emerson's advice for finding yourself is very simple: do your work, and people will know you. He says that by doing your work, you also make yourself stronger for the next task.
Emerson writes that what I must do is all that concerns me, and not what the people think. This rule is easy to say, but hard to live by, because we all want to be liked.
Emerson links self-trust to a spiritual belief: the same great spirit lives in every person. Trusting yourself, he suggests, means trusting that deeper source, so it is not the same as being selfish.
Many people lean on friends, customs, laws and money, and they never learn to stand alone. Emerson wants us to enjoy these things, but not to lean on them like crutches.
A person is calm and cheerful when he has put his heart into his work and done his best. What he has said or done in any other way, Emerson says, will never give him peace.
Near the end, Emerson lists the events that lift our spirits: a victory, higher rents, a sick friend who gets well. He tells us not to believe that these good events will bring us lasting peace.
Good luck and good news may be pleasant, but they cannot be the true source of lasting peace. Nothing can bring you peace but yourself, Emerson says, and it grows out of your own steady mind.
Emerson ends with one last thought: nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles. Trust yourself, live by what you believe is true, and you will find a calm that nobody can take away.
C1C2: Ralph Waldo Emerson, a former minister who became one of America's best-known essayists and lecturers, published Self-Reliance in 1841 in the first series of his Essays. It is a short and restless piece of writing, more like a trumpet than a lecture, and it asks every reader to stop borrowing opinions. Few essays have been quoted so often, or have so stubbornly unsettled people who prefer to be comfortable.

Emerson begins with a quiet observation: that we habitually dismiss our own inmost thoughts merely because they are ours, and then admire them when they appear in the work of a stranger. In every work of genius, he says, we recognise our own rejected ideas, returning to us with a certain alienated majesty. The lesson is that the voice we ignore may be the very one most worth heeding.

Great poems and great paintings, he suggests, do not so much teach us new things as give back to us what we had already half felt and failed to trust. We admire them because they say aloud what we were too timid to say ourselves. A person who learns this will begin to regard his own passing convictions with far more respect.

To believe that what is true for you in your own private heart is true for all people: that, in Emerson's eyes, is genius. He therefore urges us to speak our latent convictions with confidence, since what we say in secret may later prove to be the common sense of everyone. The thought that is only ours today, in other words, is often the thought that all of us will share tomorrow.

Trust yourself, Emerson declares, for every heart vibrates to that iron string, and no other voice can summon quite the same response. He asks us to accept the place that providence has found for us, the society of our contemporaries and the connection of events that make up our lives. We are not accidents, he insists, but expressions of a purpose that is waiting for us to cooperate.

The great figures of history, he points out, all did precisely this, giving their trust to the thought that was truly their own and to the work that fitted them. They did not hide behind the opinions of their age, nor did they wait for anyone's permission. We are called, in the same spirit, to stand upright in our own place and to speak from there.

To show what he means, Emerson points to the very young, who have not yet learned to measure themselves against other people. Infants and children, like animals, have a mind that is not divided, and they look upon the world with a steady and fearless gaze. Indeed, he notes, one baby in a room can make four or five grown adults forget their dignity and join in the play.

Emerson paints the portrait of a healthy boy, a youth who cannot be bribed by the praise of others and who judges people and events with fresh candour. He says what he thinks, gives or withholds his approval as he sees fit, and does not trouble himself about consequences. Somewhere in growing up, the adult world's judgement creeps in and takes this freedom away.

Society, Emerson warns, is everywhere in a kind of conspiracy against the manhood of each of its members. It resembles a company of shareholders in which every person agrees, for the sake of securing his bread, to surrender the liberty and culture of the eater. The bargain is so ordinary that most of us never notice we have signed it.

The virtue most in demand, Emerson observes, is conformity, and the quality most disliked is self-reliance, which refuses to keep step with the crowd. Society wants not realities and creators but names and customs, and it rewards the person who keeps them without question. A mind that insists on its own judgement therefore pays for the privilege in the coin of the world's displeasure.

Whoever would be a real man, he says, must be a nonconformist, and must hold nothing so sacred as the integrity of his own mind. If a person satisfies his own conscience, Emerson promises, he will in the end win the approval of the world as well. In his hands, the old idea of conscience becomes a call to look inward before looking about.

Emerson recalls the answer he once gave, as a young man, to an older adviser who kept urging on him the old doctrines of the church. When the adviser warned that such inner impulses might come from below rather than from above, Emerson replied that they did not seem to him to be of that kind. He would follow what he found true in himself, for nothing else could honestly be asked of him.

The names of good and bad, he adds, are easily moved from one thing to another, and he cannot accept a rule merely because other people accept it. Every principle must be tested in the private court of his own conscience before he will call it good. Such a stand may look arrogant, yet it asks far more honesty than obedience ever does.

It makes him ashamed, he confesses, to see how easily people yield to badges and names, to great societies and dead institutions. A stranger appears with a famous title or a respected label, and we hand over our own judgement before he has said a word. Emerson wants us to look at the thing itself, and not only at the name it wears.

It is easy, he notes, to live after the world's opinion while we are in the crowd, and easy to live after our own while we are alone in the study. The great person is the one who, in the middle of the crowd, keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude. This is the double skill that Emerson asks of us: to stand near others without becoming them.

He grows doubtful about acts of charity done merely because it is the fashion, and he says so bluntly, preferring an honest refusal to a hollow show of generosity. Kindness, in his view, must grow from real affection and a clear sight of what is needed. Goodness, he adds, should have some edge to it, or it becomes only a polite habit.

To follow customs that have gone dead for us, he argues, only scatters our force and blurs the picture that other people have of us. A day spent obeying rules in which we no longer believe is a day of strength wasted. What looks like politeness may in truth be a slow leak in the character.

Anyone who belongs to a party or a sect becomes easy to forecast, Emerson remarks, for if he knows your side, he can guess your argument before you have opened your mouth. The speaker's real mind is then replaced by the opinions of the group, and his face, like his talk, takes on a stiff and forced expression. It is a very high price to pay for the comfort of belonging to a crowd.

Nonconformity, he cautions, is paid for with the world's displeasure, and the fear of disapproval is perhaps the strongest chain that holds us. A man must therefore learn how to estimate a sour face at its true value, which is far smaller than it seems. Once the frown has been weighed, he suggests, it hardly weighs anything at all.

Many of us hold back from changing our minds for fear of seeming inconsistent, but Emerson has little patience with this anxiety. A foolish consistency, he declares, is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen, philosophers and divines. The adjective matters: he is mocking the stubborn habit of repeating yesterday's words, and not the steady practice of honest thought.

Speak what you think today in blunt, unpolished words, he says, and tomorrow speak what tomorrow thinks in equally plain words, though it contradict everything you said today. The advice is deliberately shocking, yet it rests on a simple respect for the truth as it appears from one moment to the next. A mind that truly grows will inevitably leave many of its old statements far behind it.

Is it really so terrible, he asks, to be misunderstood by the people around us, when so many of the wise were? Pythagoras, Socrates, Jesus, Luther, Copernicus, Galileo and Newton were all misunderstood in their own day, along with every pure and wise spirit that has ever lived among us. To be great, Emerson concludes, is to be misunderstood, and the discomfort of it is a sign of company worth keeping.

Life, he suggests, does not run along a ruled line, and a good life seen from close at hand may look confused and contradictory. The voyage of the best ship is a zigzag line of a hundred tacks, yet when it is viewed from a sufficient distance, it straightens itself into the average tendency. In the same way, honest actions that seem to disagree will turn out to belong to a single direction.

He asks us to live for ourselves and not as a spectacle for others, preferring a life of a plainer note that is genuine and steady to one that is glittering and unsteady. Great displays, in his view, soon tire both the performer and the watching audience alike. A modest but honest day, spent on what is truly one's own, is worth more than a brilliant day spent on being seen.

Genuine actions, Emerson promises, will explain themselves and will also explain each other, so we need not anxiously defend each one in turn. The person who acts from a settled centre does not require a lawyer to prove that his deeds belong together. Over time, the pattern that others could not at first see becomes plain to everyone who looks.

Every great person is a unique character, Emerson says, and the very thing that makes him great is the part of him that could not have been borrowed. The glory of a general or a saint lies precisely in what he alone brought to the work, and it cannot be copied by those who follow. We honour the great best, therefore, by becoming our own selves rather than their shadows.

There comes a time in every person's education, Emerson says, when he is convinced that envy is ignorance and that imitation is a kind of suicide. He must accept himself, for better or worse, because the wide universe is full of good, yet no nourishing grain will come to him except by his own toil upon the ground he was given. It is one of the most quoted passages in the essay, and it is easy to see why.

So he urges us to insist on ourselves and never to imitate, for our own gift we can present at every moment with the force of a whole life's cultivation. The talent we merely adopt from another is held only by half, and it never quite sits easy in the hand. Better a small voice that is truly ours than a grand one that has been learned by heart.

The roses under his window, Emerson says, make no reference to former roses or to better ones; they are for what they are, and they exist with God today. There is no time to them, only the full presence of the flower in the moment of its blooming. A rose at its first opening is as complete as it will ever be.

A human being, by contrast, postpones or remembers, and with a backward glance laments the past or, heedless of the riches that surround him, stands on tiptoe to foresee the future. He cannot be happy and strong, Emerson argues, until he too lives with nature in the present, above time. The remedy for regret and worry is thus the simplest of all: to attend to what is here.

Emerson trusts the first swift sense of what is true, which he names instinct or intuition, and which he says we do not learn from teachers or from books. The deeper we follow it toward its source, the more it seems to lie beneath argument, in a place where reasons have not yet begun. For this reason, he asks that we honour such moments of clear seeing, and not explain them away afterward.

His remarks on prayer may surprise readers who expect a gentler tone, for he judges any prayer that begs for some particular favour to be mistaken. The only true prayer, in his view, is the contemplation of the facts of life from the highest point of view. In this respect he speaks as a reformer of religious habit, and not as an enemy of the spirit.

Discontent, Emerson says, is the want of self-reliance, an infirmity of the will, and the person who is forever complaining has not yet learned to rely on his own powers. We are tempted to blame circumstance, our neighbours or the age for our unease, when the cure lies closer to hand. He means this as a challenge, though it may also be received as a comfort.

An institution, he writes, is the lengthened shadow of one man, and the great movements of the world began as the strong convictions of single persons. Luther's Reformation and Wesley's Methodism are among the examples that he offers, each of them the long shadow of a single man. If we revere the shadow and forget the man who cast it, we have learned very little from either.

He now turns to travel, which he calls a fool's paradise when it is undertaken to escape from ourselves. Emerson has no objection to a journey made for art, for study or for kindness, so long as the traveller is first at home in his own mind. But the soul, he insists, is no traveller, and the wise person stays at home with it.

A man who travels to be amused, or to obtain something that he does not carry within him, travels away from himself, Emerson warns, and grows old among old things in a foreign land. He imagines packing his trunk, embracing his friends and sailing to Naples, only to wake up one morning and find at his side the same sad self that he had fled. No distance, in other words, is great enough to leave behind a restless mind.

The intellect is a vagabond, he claims, and our system of education fosters restlessness, because our minds travel while our bodies are forced to stay at home. We imitate, and what is imitation, he asks, but the travelling of the mind? Whole nations of readers borrow their houses, their taste and their opinions from abroad, and then wonder why nothing feels their own.

Emerson also warns against placing too much trust in property, which he regards as one of the great substitutes for trust in oneself. He says that people have looked at things for so long that they value schools, churches and laws mainly as guards of property, and judge one another by what each has rather than by what each is. A man who has nothing but his possessions, he implies, has not much to stand on.

The reliance on property, including the reliance on the governments that protect it, he calls the want of self-reliance. A person who has taught himself to feel safe only when his wealth is safe has given the key of his peace into someone else's hand. Real security, Emerson insists, has to be grown within, where no tax collector or thief can reach it.

Emerson then makes a claim that surprises many readers: society never advances, but recedes as fast on one side as it gains on the other. It passes through many changes, being barbarous, then civilised, then rich and scientific, yet this change, he says, is not true improvement. For every new power that people gain, they lose some skill or strength that had once been their own.

The civilised man, he writes, has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet; he is supported on crutches, but lacks so much support of muscle. He possesses a fine Geneva watch, yet fails of the skill to tell the hour by the sun. His careful almanac tells him where the stars are, and so the man in the street no longer knows a star in the sky.

Society, Emerson says, is a wave: the wave moves onward, but the water of which it is composed does not. The unity of the form is only an appearance, and the individual people who make it up are no better for the passage of the swell. It is the person, and not the age in which he lives, that has to be improved if anything is to change.

Emerson's advice for finding out who you are is very plain: do your work, and I shall know you. Do your work, he continues, and you shall reinforce yourself, as a person who has made something grows steadier with every finished task. Talk and theory fade quickly from memory, but the finished work stands and speaks in your name.

It is not easy to ignore the opinions of others, and Emerson never pretends that it is. What I must do is all that concerns me, he writes, and not what the people think, a rule that is equally hard in action and in thought. We want to be liked, and the whole craft of living freely lies in loving the truth a little more.

Beneath all this, Emerson holds a quiet religious conviction: that the same spirit lives in every person, and that its voice is what we hear when we are most ourselves. To trust oneself, in his view, is therefore to trust that deeper source, and it cannot be mistaken for mere selfishness. He writes as one who believes that reverence and independence are not enemies but partners.

Most of us lean upon friends, customs, laws and money, and we never discover whether our own legs would carry us. Emerson would have us enjoy these supports without making crutches of them, and so remain upright even when they are taken away. The test of a person is not what he can do with every help, but what he can do with none.

A man is relieved and gay when he has put his heart into his work and done his best, Emerson writes, but what he has said or done otherwise shall give him no peace. Applause cannot comfort us when we know that we gave less than we had, nor can criticism wound us when we gave all. The reward lies in the effort itself, and the effort, for better or worse, is entirely our own.

Near the end he lists the events that raise our spirits: a political victory, a rise of rents, the recovery of a sick friend, the return of an absent one. We think that good days are being prepared for us, but Emerson says flatly that we should not believe it. No outside event, however welcome, can supply the quiet that only the mind itself can provide.

Nothing can bring you peace but yourself, he says, in a sentence so plain that it is easy to read past without feeling its weight. The comforts of fortune are pleasant and may be gratefully received, yet they pass, and the person who depended on them is left once more with an unsettled heart. Peace, if it comes, is built from within, stone by stone, by a mind that has chosen to be at home in itself.

Emerson closes with a last and carefully chosen thought: nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles. Trust yourself, then, and live by what you hold to be true, even when the crowd, the fashion and your own fears advise otherwise. The essay is nearly two centuries old, but its demand remains fresh, and it is addressed, as it always was, to each of us alone.
